newsitem.title: TAIWAN: One year on, Taiwan's Lee faces heavy going.
newsitem.headline: One year on, Taiwan's Lee faces heavy going.

text.p: What a difference one year can make.

Last May, when Taiwan's people spilled into the streets, it was to revel in their new-found democracy and cheer the man who had come to personify it -- Lee Teng-hui, winner in March of the first popular presidential election in Chinese history.

Hundreds of thousands came out for Lee's swearing-in on May 20, 1996, singing, chanting, beating drums and proudly waving flags of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China in parades in many parts of the island.

Not only had Lee helped dismantle martial law and proved that multiparty democracy could work in a Chinese society, he did so in heroic style with a campaign based on defiance of arch rival communist China, which had mounted months of nerve-jangling war games in a bid to weaken Lee's support.

China's missile tests backfired badly, drawing a muscular response from the United States, which dispatched two aircraft carrier groups to waters near Taiwan in a move that startled Beijing and eased Taiwan's sense of isolation.
Between tears of joy, Taiwan cheered and cheered.
How times have changed. A year later, Taiwan citizens again have been swarming in the streets -- but their angry message leaves no doubt that the charismatic Lee's honeymoon is over.

A noisy but peaceful throng estimated at anywhere between 30,000 and 100,000 marched on Taipei's Presidential Office on Sunday, demanding Lee take the blame for government bumbling -- most notably a perception that law and order has collapsed.
Critics urge Lee to show sincerity by sacking Premier Lien Chan, his hand-picked cabinet chief and presumed choice to stand for election in 2000 to succeed the president.
"The best way for President Lee to show his concern is to replace the premier immediately," said Lin Yi-hsiung, a protest organiser from the opposition Democratic Progressive Party.
Unwelcome news has sloshed in from all over.

--Stalwart allies South Africa and the Bahamas are switching diplomatic ties to Beijing, fanning fears that Panama, Guatemala and others may too. Taiwan has ties with only 30 states, most of them small, poor and reliant on Taipei's financial largesse.

--A multibillion-dollar hog-farm epidemic has all but erased a hard-won economic recovery engineered since October. Taiwan has had to pare back its 1997 gross domestic product growth forecast despite a surprisingly big first-quarter rise.

--Despite a bold crackdown on organised crime, public unease has soared, stoked in good part by the police failure to crack a spate of horrific crimes, from the gangland-style execution of a county magistrate and seven associates to the kidnap, torture and murder of a celebrity's teenaged daughter.

--Dissent has come even from ranks of Lee's once-indomitable political machine. Fresh-faced "golden boy" Ma Ying-jeou, tipped by pollsters as the Nationalist Party's best chance to win the Taipei mayoralty back from the Democratic Progressives, has quit the cabinet and announced he would not run.
Though public anger largely has been directed at Premier Lien, Lee has become a target as well.
Critics have turned up their attacks on Nationalist-proposed constitutional reforms currently under review that many warn will boost Lee's clout at parliament's expense.

Citizens who have soured on Lee's leadership increasingly have been mobilised by the three main opposition parties and a welter of independent pressure groups that organised Sunday's huge march and a similar protest two weeks ago.
"Admit your errors," said a slogan beamed by lasers onto the tower jutting from Lee's downtown office building.
Marchers carried placards reading "fury", "take a hike", "apologise" and "step down".
Little wonder, then, that President Lee will not be spending Tuesday, the first anniversary of his gala inauguration, crowing in public about his successes.
Rather, he'll be in his hometown of Sanchih outside Taipei, humbly sweeping the floors at a home for the elderly -- a traditional act of quiet contrition and filial piety.
